chapter: A finite search, with a reason to succeed

sentences.text: Part Two ended with a certificate: a justified interval whose lower endpoint is above zero.
Now we want a program to find such a certificate and tell us where it found it.
That sounds like a loop over some sample points.
But a loop can finish without finding anything.
Our task has three separate parts: construct a finite list of addresses… inspect their interval bounds… and prove that an address must be found when the hypotheses hold.
We will follow one example all the way through.
A peak sits between grid points, and the program sees only the rational intervals supplied at the grid addresses.
It will not know the location of the peak by magic.
Instead, a bound on how much the values can fall, together with enough numerical precision, will force at least one interval to pass the test.
This is Part Three of Landau Windows ACL Two: a finite search that must succeed.
As before, the computed objects and the mathematical guarantees will both appear on screen.

chapter: Inspect the lower endpoints in order

sentences.text: Begin with four sample intervals, in a fixed order.
The threshold is zero, and the test asks whether a lower endpoint is strictly greater than that threshold.
The first interval runs from minus seven eighths to minus five eighths.
Its lower endpoint fails the test… so move to the next interval.
The second lower endpoint, minus three eighths, fails too.
The third interval runs from one eighth to three eighths.
Its lower endpoint is positive… so this is our first qualifying sample.
The fourth interval also has a positive lower endpoint, but this scan stops at the first success.
We number the positions from zero.
So the qualifying interval is at index two, even though it is the third interval we inspected.
An index is a position in a list; we will distinguish it from the numerical grid address.
Every comparison in this example is an exact rational comparison.
Here is the actual definition of lw-first-above, from the repository.
We will read it in two cards, so the complete code stays legible.
The inputs are a threshold and a list of sample intervals.
We are working with proper finite lists, ending in nil.
On these lists, endp detects that there are no samples left; the function then returns nil.
Nil will be our signal that the scan found no qualifying interval.
Otherwise, the composed accessor caar takes the first interval… and then its lower endpoint.
The next if compares that endpoint with the threshold.
If it passes, cons returns index zero paired with that first interval.
Now continue the same definition on the second card.
The recursive call scans the remaining list, obtained with cdr.
Let gives that returned result the temporary name found.
If the recursive call failed, return nil again.
If it succeeded, add one to its index and keep its interval.
That addition translates an index in the shorter tail back into an index in the original list.
When we fold the cards into the function name, all of that behavior is what the name abbreviates.

chapter: An index is not a grid address

sentences.text: Unwind the successful call in our example.
In the tail that starts at the qualifying interval, the answer has index zero.
Returning through one earlier interval changes that index to one… and returning through the next changes it to two.
The interval itself stays the interval from one eighth to three eighths.
The printed result is a pair: index two, followed by that interval.
Car retrieves the index… and cdr retrieves the interval.
Nil means failure, but the number zero does not mean failure in ACL2.
In particular, a result beginning with index zero is still a successful pair.
Now put the grid addresses beside the samples.
The first three addresses are zero, one eighth, and one quarter.
The ACL2 operation nth uses a zero-based index to select an item.
So index two selects the address one quarter.
The returned index and the address have different jobs: one identifies a position, and the other identifies where we sampled.

chapter: Why a returned certificate is sound

sentences.text: Finding an index is useful only if we can justify what it identifies.
The repository proves that a successful result has a natural-number index within the sample list.
It also proves that the returned interval is the interval at that index.
Those are statements about the search's bookkeeping.
To relate the interval to a value, we need one more input guarantee.
The function lw-encloses-values pairs each sample interval with its corresponding rational value.
At each position, lw-contains checks the enclosure we defined in Part Two, and the function recurses on the two tails.
When the lists end, their lengths must agree in the sense expressed by the base case.
This guarantee is not supplied by the search itself.
Given those enclosures, a returned lower endpoint above the threshold forces the corresponding value above the threshold.
The theorem lw-first-above-value-gt expresses that implication using nth at the returned index.
A successful computation therefore gives a checkable certificate… provided the input intervals really enclose the values.
The eventual application must establish that premise.
Why does this scan terminate?
Every recursive call discards one interval, so the remaining list is shorter.
That is a natural-number measure that cannot decrease forever.
It is the same finite-descent idea behind the recursive proofs in Part Zero.
But termination alone does not promise a successful result.
Consider a grid containing only the two endpoints of the unit interval.
The function in our illustration has a positive peak between those addresses, while both endpoint values are negative.
Even perfectly justified, narrow intervals at those two endpoints can fail the positivity test.
The scan finishes and returns nil.
This does not contradict the existence of the peak.
It shows why a complete argument needs control of the gaps between samples… and control of how far the value can fall across a gap.
The triangular curve here is our explicit teaching example, not a computed plot of the Landau statistic.
Let us build the addresses instead of leaving them implicit.
Our teaching constructor takes a count, a starting address, and a step.
If the count is zero, it returns the empty list.
Otherwise it stores the starting address and continues with one fewer point, starting one step farther along.
Here is the complete definition of video-uniform-grid.
For natural counts, this recursion produces exactly that many addresses.
With nine points, starting at zero and using a step of one eighth, the final address is one.
Notice the counting: nine points leave eight gaps.
Each address is rational when the start and step are rational.
We can refine this picture by changing a step of one half… to one quarter… and then one eighth, increasing the point count accordingly.
This constructor is for the lesson; the project's later window construction has additional endpoint and rounding obligations.
Nothing about writing a finite loop by itself proves that the resulting grid is fine enough.

chapter: State what the grid must guarantee

sentences.text: We need an exact condition on the list of addresses.
The repository calls it lw-meshp.
It requires a nonempty list of rational addresses, written in increasing order with equality allowed.
Each consecutive gap must be at most the supplied mesh bound.
The next recursive call checks the same requirements along the rest of the list.
The final branch checks that the list ends properly.
The complete definition is shown in two cards.
We also need to name the last address, so here is the short definition of lw-last-address.
That function follows the tail until only the final address remains.
The teaching book proves that our uniform constructor satisfies the mesh condition when the count is positive, the start and step are rational, and the step is nonnegative.
This is a general constructor guarantee, not just a check of the nine displayed points.
For the worked example, the mesh bound is one eighth.

chapter: A point inside the span has a nearby sample

sentences.text: What does the mesh condition buy us?
Take any rational point between the first and last addresses.
If it is itself a grid address, the distance to a sample can be zero.
If it lies inside a gap, that gap is at most the mesh bound.
So at least one of its bordering addresses is within that bound.
We only need this conservative distance bound; we are not claiming the smallest possible distance.
The predicate lw-some-nearby records that at least one listed address has distance at most the mesh bound from the point.
Abs means absolute value, the distance from zero, so absolute address minus point measures their separation.
The theorem lw-mesh-covers-point combines the sorted-gap condition with the requirement that the point lies inside the grid's span.
In our example, the peak is at seven sixteenths, between three eighths and one half.
Either of those neighboring addresses is close enough.
This geometric guarantee still says nothing about the sampled values until we add a bound on their possible drop.

chapter: How much can a nearby value fall?

sentences.text: Now supply that bound.
Suppose the peak value is one, and the value can fall by at most four times the distance moved away from the peak.
Four is the rate bound in our example.
A move of one eighth can therefore lose at most one half.
This is the useful part of a Lipschitz bound: distance controls possible change in value.
We only need a lower bound on the sampled values, not equality with the sides of the drawn triangle.
The arithmetic condition is: sample value is at least peak minus rate times distance from the peak's point.
The function lw-lower-lipschitz checks that condition at every listed address and its corresponding rational value.
Here is its complete definition, continued onto a second card.
The first checks keep the address and value lists aligned, and require rational entries.
The inequality on the second card is the lower bound we just drew.
The recursive call repeats it for the remaining entries.
A theorem about search can use this as a hypothesis; the search cannot manufacture such a bound by looking at finitely many intervals.
The larger mathematical application must prove it.

chapter: Budget both spatial loss and interval width

sentences.text: A nearby value can remain positive while a loose interval still crosses zero.
So there are two losses to budget.
The first is spatial: rate times the mesh bound.
The second is numerical: the full width allowed for each enclosure.
The function lw-widths-at-most checks that width requirement over the sample list.
Its composed accessor takes the upper endpoint of the first interval, and subtracts the lower endpoint.
Then it continues through the remaining intervals.
This budget is a full width, not the midpoint error radius we distinguished in Part Two.
For our example, the width budget is one quarter.
Each displayed enclosure is centered on its exact teaching value with a radius of one eighth, so its full width is one quarter.
The two quantities are consistent, but they are not interchangeable.
We also keep the enclosure premise: a narrow interval around the wrong value would not help.

chapter: Why the margin forces a qualifying interval

sentences.text: Here is the central inequality.
The peak must be strictly above the threshold, plus the spatial-loss budget, plus the interval-width budget.
In our example the threshold is zero… the rate is four… the mesh is one eighth… and the width budget is one quarter.
The total budget is three quarters, which is strictly below the peak value one.
Coverage supplies a nearby address.
The rate bound then places its value above the threshold plus the width budget.
The predicate lw-some-value-above expresses that at least one listed rational value exceeds a supplied level.
Now use Part Two's margin lemma: a containing interval this narrow must have its lower endpoint above the threshold.
So there is at least one interval that passes the scan's test.
The function lw-some-lower-above expresses that last existence claim directly in terms of lower endpoints.
Its definition follows the same list structure as the search.
The search's completeness theorem says that the scan returns a non-nil result exactly when such a lower endpoint exists.
That is the difference between hoping to find a sample… and proving that the finite scan cannot miss all of them.

chapter: Read the hypotheses of the full guarantee

sentences.text: The repository combines those steps in lw-grid-search-complete.
We will read its complete source across four cards.
The opening hypotheses state the rational domains, including the point, peak, rate, mesh, threshold, and error budget.
Next come nonnegativity of the rate and mesh, and the actual mesh condition on the addresses.
The point must lie between the first and last addresses.
The strict margin pays for both the rate-times-mesh loss and the full enclosure width.
The sampled values must satisfy the lower transport bound.
The intervals must enclose those values, and all their widths must meet the budget.
Under those hypotheses, the conclusion is that lw-first-above returns a successful result.
The lines marked hints tell ACL2 which already proved lemmas to use; they are instructions to the prover, not extra mathematical hypotheses.
The final card completes those proof instructions.
This is a conditional success theorem.
It does not assert that every grid finds every peak, or that every numerical estimate is already justified.
It states exactly which supplied guarantees make this finite search succeed.
All values in this checked statement are rational; connecting the construction to the intended analytic objects remains an explicit interpretation obligation.
Let us check the whole chain in the example we have been building.
The point is seven sixteenths, the peak is one, and the rate bound is four.
The grid runs from zero to one in steps of one eighth.
The values shown are exactly one minus four times the absolute distance from seven sixteenths.
Each interval contains its displayed value and has full width one quarter.
The mesh condition, the span condition, and the strict margin all hold.
The peak's neighboring samples are at three eighths and one half.
But the scan does not have to return the closest address to the peak.
It examines the list from the beginning… skips the two negative lower endpoints… and accepts the next interval.
The returned index is two, and selecting that position in the address list gives one quarter.
The certified interval there is from one eighth to three eighths, containing the value one quarter.
That lower endpoint proves the value is positive.
The teaching book checks the numerical premises and this exact returned result.
The general theorem explains why some success was forced, independently of watching this particular animation.

chapter: What a failed scan does and does not say

sentences.text: One last distinction matters for the later Landau argument.
A result of nil means that none of the supplied lower endpoints passed the test.
It does not, by itself, mean that every underlying value is below the threshold.
A positive value of one eighth can sit inside an interval from minus one eighth to three eighths.
That interval contains the value, but its lower endpoint fails the test.
Here the width is one half, so a margin greater than that width is unavailable.
The completeness theorem prevents this failure only when all its hypotheses hold.
Conversely, if a computation fails, we cannot keep all those hypotheses and still claim the required strict peak margin.
The larger proof must specify which hypotheses have already been established before using such reasoning.
We have separated the scan, the accuracy of its inputs, and the mathematical reason that a sample must qualify.
Those are different obligations, and each now has a place in the argument.

chapter: The search is ready for a real signal

sentences.text: We can now construct a finite grid and inspect exact rational intervals.
A successful result identifies a genuine interval in the list and a position we can translate into a grid address.
The mesh condition supplies coverage, the rate bound controls spatial loss, and the width budget controls numerical uncertainty.
A strict margin connects those guarantees to a search that must succeed.
These are reusable arithmetic statements, expressed in ACL2 and connected to the Peano Arithmetic goal through explicit finite representations.
We have not yet explained how the prime-counting signal supplies all those inputs.
That is the next step.
In Part Four, we start with prime powers and build the smoothed signal whose intervals the later search will inspect.
The machinery from this episode tells us what that evaluator must deliver.
The eventual Landau theorem still requires the mathematical hypotheses and the interpretation of the complete construction.
